notes.meaning: Pilate refused to change the inscription he placed above the cross. He was annoyed with the Jewish leaders for pressuring him and was determined not to yield to them any further. God used Pilate's stubbornness so that Jesus was openly proclaimed as King, a title that would stand forever.

Four Roman soldiers carried out the crucifixion and divided Jesus' outer clothes into four shares. His inner tunic, however, had no seams and was woven in one single piece from top to bottom. This special tunic resembled the vestment worn by the high priest under the Old Testament law.

The soldiers decided not to tear the seamless tunic, but threw dice to see who would win it. Without knowing it, they fulfilled Psalm 22:18, which foretold that men would divide His clothes and cast lots for His garment. Even the careless greed of Roman soldiers proved that God was directing every detail of the cross.

A small group of faithful women stood right near the cross as Jesus suffered. They showed great courage and devotion by staying close to Him when most of His disciples had run away. Their quiet love gave comfort to Jesus in His darkest hour.

Jesus looked down from the cross and saw His mother Mary standing beside the apostle John. He told Mary to look on John as her son, and told John to take care of Mary as his own mother. Even while bearing the sins of the world, Jesus lovingly provided a safe home for His widowed mother.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Mary is seen as being given to the apostle John to be the spiritual mother of all believers, and the entrustment indicates that Mary had no other biological children.

notes.meaning: Jesus knew that His great mission of redeeming mankind was now almost fully accomplished. To fulfill Psalm 69:21, which spoke of the Messiah's suffering, He said aloud, "I am thirsty." His words showed the real physical torment of the cross and His total commitment to completing Scripture.

A jar of sour wine, the cheap drink used by Roman soldiers, was sitting nearby. A soldier soaked a sponge in the wine, placed it on a hyssop branch, and raised it to Jesus' mouth. This relieved His dry lips so He could speak His final words with clarity.

After tasting the sour wine, Jesus cried out in victory, "It is finished." He meant that the punishment for sin was fully paid, the ancient prophecies were fulfilled, and the work of salvation was complete. Then He bowed His head and willingly gave up His spirit into the hands of His Father.

The Jewish leaders asked Pilate to break the legs of the crucified men so they would die quickly and could be taken down before evening. A special Sabbath was starting at sunset, and they did not want the land defiled by bodies hanging on crosses. In their hypocrisy, they worried about outward calendar rules while feeling no guilt over killing the Son of God.

Soldiers came with heavy clubs and broke the legs of the two criminals, making it impossible for them to breathe and ending their lives. But when they reached Jesus, they saw He had already died, so they did not break His legs. God's watchful care protected His Son's body from being broken by human violence.

A soldier drove a spear into Jesus' side to make certain He was really dead, and blood and water immediately poured out. This deep wound confirmed that Jesus had truly passed away and had not merely fainted on the cross. The blood and water also pictured the forgiveness and spiritual cleansing He won for all who trust Him.

John wrote down these events as an eyewitness who stood right by the cross and watched the spear strike Jesus' side. He gave this honest testimony so that all who read it would firmly believe in Jesus. Our faith rests on real historical events witnessed by reliable men.

These events fulfilled two ancient prophecies from the Old Testament. The unbroken bones matched the rule for the Passover lamb in Exodus 12:46, and the pierced side fulfilled Zechariah 12:10. Even the rough actions of Roman executioners proved that Jesus was the true sacrifice promised by God.

Joseph of Arimathea had followed Jesus secretly because he was afraid of what the Jewish rulers might do to him. When Jesus died, Joseph found bold courage, went straight to Pilate, and asked for the body. Pilate gave him permission, allowing Joseph to rescue the body from being tossed into a common ditch.

Nicodemus, the ruler who had once met Jesus privately under cover of darkness, joined Joseph to help bury Him. He brought about seventy-five pounds of costly, fragrant spices to honor the Lord. Both men stepped forward in the open when following Jesus seemed most dangerous.

Joseph and Nicodemus washed Jesus' wounded body and wrapped it in clean linen cloths packed with the sweet-smelling spices. They buried Him with great honor and tenderness, following the customs of the Jewish people. They gave their Master the royal dignity He deserved, even in death.

Near the place where Jesus was crucified, there was a garden with a brand-new tomb cut out of the solid rock. No corpse had ever rested inside it before. This ensured that when Jesus rose, no one could claim another person had come back to life instead of Him.

Because the Sabbath was about to begin at sundown and the garden tomb was close at hand, they placed Jesus' body inside it. God guided their steps so that an honorable resting place was ready just as time ran out. There the Lord rested in peace until His glorious resurrection on the third day.
